outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version that preserves the poem's imagery, references, and emotional register while refining its language and flow:

---

In this moment of orangutans, wolves, and scavengers, of scorching heat reshaping the north and south poles, of new tribes wandering in limousines, of liars, thieves, and con artists confirmed to power—in this wilderness of Pennsylvania Avenue, of Standing Rock, of misspelled executive orders scrawled on yellow paper with crooked signatures—where are the kind language-makers among us?

In this age of catastrophic climate damage, of deciphering fake news, alternative truths, and rampant self-interest, you foresaw the twenty-first century and left us—not by your own choice or consent. You fought, relentlessly, through most of the twentieth century, raising an army of poets who learned to love language and the stories of complicated rivers, seas, and oceans. Where now is the kind, green nourishment of kale and wheatgrass?

You thought, wrote, and lived poetry. You knew that terror, too, is a language—rooted in denial, in supremacy, in the cowardice of the rich. You were honey and yes to us. You never fled from Blackness—from bones, from Africa, from blood, from the hard questioning of yesterdays and tomorrows. We never saw you dance, yet you carried rhythm in your bones. You were a warrior before the war, forging an earth-language of uncommon signs and melodies, refusing to sing the songs of career slaves.

Keenly aware of Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, Du Bois—of the vast consciousness and unyielding commitment of those who never quit, who bore devout witness to the bloodlust of kindness's enemies—we hear your final words:

*America, if you see me as your enemy, you have no friends.*

In this era marked by primates, predators, and opportunistic vultures, when scorching temperatures reshape the Arctic and Antarctic, and fresh convoys of privilege cruise by in stretch cars, when charlatans, swindlers, and con artists receive official approval—amid the chaos of Pennsylvania Avenue, at Standing Rock, where poorly spelled decrees appear on yellow legal pads bearing crooked signatures—where have the gentle wordsmiths gone?

During this age of severe environmental destruction, of untangling manufactured news, distorted realities, and self-obsession, you witnessed the arrival of the twenty-first century and departed us, though not by choice or consent. Throughout most of the twentieth century, you battled relentlessly, building a generation of poets devoted to language and to stories flowing through tangled rivers, seas, and oceans.

Where now is the gentle nourishment—the green sustenance of kale and wheatgrass? You embodied poetry in thought, in writing, in living; you understood that terror, too, speaks a language rooted in denial, in supremacist thinking, and in the cowardice of the wealthy. To us, you were sweetness and affirmation, never shying from Blackness—from bones, from Africa, from bloodlines, from interrogating both history and what lies ahead.

We never watched you dance, yet rhythm lived within you; you were a fighter before any battle began, forging an earthbound language, unfamiliar symbols and tunes, refusing to perform the anthems of those enslaved by ambition. Deeply conscious of Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, Du Bois, and the vast awareness and dedication of those who refuse surrender, faithfully tracking the enemies of compassion who thirst for blood—we now hear your final words:

America, if you view me as your enemy, then you have no friends at all.

# The Weight of Witness: A Reading of the Tribute Poem

The poem opens into a landscape of crisis—a world destabilized by corrupt leadership, environmental collapse, and the slow poisoning of public discourse through misinformation and rampant self-interest. This is not a gentle or nostalgic space; it is charged with urgency, depicting a political moment where truth itself has become a casualty, where those in power seem more invested in personal gain than in the collective good, and where the natural world bears the scars of human negligence. Against this backdrop of chaos, the poem does not retreat into despair but instead turns toward a figure whose life work stands as a counterforce to this unraveling.

That figure is a poet who gave the better part of a century to the discipline and possibility of language itself. This was not merely a solitary artistic pursuit but a generative, communal act—the poet is remembered as a mentor who cultivated what the text calls an "army of poets," a phrase that suggests both militancy and multitude. These are writers trained not in easy narratives but in the difficult work of excavating "complicated histories and landscapes," inheriting a responsibility to tell stories that resist simplification.

Central to the tribute is a nuanced understanding of fear and violence. The poem insists that this figure recognized terror not as some abstract or external force, but as something intimately human—born из denial, nurtured by privilege, and sustained by cowardice. This clear-eyed diagnosis of terror's roots did not curdle into bitterness or cynicism. Instead, the poet remained, paradoxically and powerfully, a wellspring of warmth and affirmation. There was no flinching from the realities of Black identity and history; rather, the poet met these realities with steady, loving attention, refusing both erasure and easy comfort.

The poem elevates this figure beyond the role of mere wordsmith, casting them instead as warrior and visionary. Rather than settling into safe, marketable, or conventionally palatable modes of storytelling, this poet forged what the text calls "earth language"—an elemental, urgent, and original mode of expression. This is language that breaks from commercial expectation, language rooted in something deeper and more primal than trend or trade, language meant to endure and to challenge.

In its closing movement, the poem situates this poet within a lineage of Black liberation—invoking Harriet Tubman, Frederick Douglass, Ida B. Wells-Barnett, and W.E.B. Du Bois. This genealogy is not incidental; it frames the poet as inheritor and continuer of a moral and political tradition dedicated to freedom, truth-telling, and justice. The poem's final gesture is a warning, direct and unambiguous, addressed to America itself: to treat such a figure—one who bears witness with unflinching moral clarity—as an enemy is to invite consequence, to court a reckoning long foretold by history.

# In Memory of a Truth-Teller: A Eulogy for the Ages

## The Weight of a Departed Voice

We gather in this moment—an era where the machinery of political corruption grinds on unabated, where environmental catastrophe looms as both slow violence and sudden reckoning, where deception has become so rampant that truth itself feels like a radical act—to mourn the passing of a poet-elder whose entire life's work stood in direct opposition to these very forces. This eulogistic poem does not simply commemorate a death; it bears witness to a legacy forged in the fires of resistance, mentorship, and unflinching honesty.

## A Life Devoted to Truth

For decades, this poet-elder dedicated the bulk of their existence to something larger than individual artistic achievement. They became a teacher, a guide, a spiritual and intellectual mentor to an entire generation of emerging poets. But theirs was not mentorship rooted in craft alone—meter, imagery, technique. Instead, they taught through language itself as a vessel for truth, insisting that words carry weight only when anchored in reality, in history, in the lived experience of struggle.

Central to their pedagogy was an unwavering commitment to Black history—not as abstract curriculum, but as living memory, as blood-knowledge passed from elder to student. They understood that to write honestly in America was to reckon with the specific violences and specific resiliences of Black experience, and they refused to let that history be sanitized, forgotten, or co-opted. Every lesson they imparted carried the understanding that poetry could be a weapon against erasure, a tool for remembering what power structures wanted forgotten.

## The Warrior Against Denial

What makes this tribute so significant is its framing of the departed not merely as a gentle mentor or beloved artist, but as a *warrior*—a fighter who spent their life in active combat against denial and injustice. This was not passive observation of society's ills but active, sustained resistance. They named corruption when others stayed silent. They spoke of environmental devastation when comfortable silence would have been easier. They called out deception in all its forms, refusing the seductive comfort of looking away.

This warrior identity matters because it reframes the poet's legacy—not as someone who simply wrote beautiful verses about difficult subjects, but as someone who understood language as a battlefield, where every honest word was a strike against the forces of oblivion and false comfort. Their poetry was not decoration; it was defense, offense, and testimony all at once.

## The Final Warning

Perhaps most haunting is the poem's culmination: the departed's final warning to America, delivered as though from beyond the grave, as though their last breath carried prophecy. This warning speaks directly to the cost of a nation that treats its truth-tellers as enemies—that punishes honesty, silences dissent, and turns away from those brave enough to name what others refuse to see.

This final message serves as both elegy and admonition. It mourns not just the loss of this individual poet-elder, but implicitly mourns what happens to any society that fails to protect and honor its truth-tellers. The warning suggests a reckoning yet to come, a cost that will be paid—perhaps already being paid—for America's historical pattern of marginalizing, dismissing, or destroying those who speak uncomfortable truths.

## Conclusion: A Legacy That Demands Continuation

This eulogistic poem, then, functions on multiple levels simultaneously: it is personal mourning for a specific individual, communal tribute to a mentor who shaped countless poetic voices, historical marker acknowledging someone's contribution to preserving Black history through art, and political warning about the dangerous consequences of silencing truth in an age of corruption and deception.

The poet-elder may be gone, but the tribute insists their warrior spirit, their commitment to truth-telling, and their final warning must not be forgotten. Their death becomes not an ending but a charge—a call to those they mentored, and to all who encounter their words, to continue the fight against denial, to keep telling truth even when it's dangerous, and to heed the warning about what happens when truth-tellers are treated as threats rather than treasures.

# Black Africa: A Continent of Diversity and Legacy

Africa is a continent of extraordinary diversity, home to thousands of ethnic groups, languages, and cultures. When people refer to "Black Africa," they typically mean the regions south of the Sahara Desert, where the majority of the population is of Black African descent. This distinguishes it from North Africa, where Arab and Berber populations predominate.

Sub-Saharan Africa encompasses an immense range of societies, from the Sahel region to the rainforests of Central Africa, the savannas of East Africa, and the diverse landscapes of Southern Africa. Countries like Nigeria, Ethiopia, Kenya, Ghana, South Africa, and the Democratic Republic of Congo each carry their own rich histories, traditions, and contributions to global civilization.

**Historical Significance**

Africa is widely recognized as the birthplace of humanity, with archaeological evidence tracing human origins back millions of years on this continent. Ancient African civilizations—such as the kingdoms of Mali, Songhai, Great Zimbabwe, Aksum, and Benin—developed sophisticated systems of governance, trade networks, and cultural achievements long before European contact.

The transatlantic slave trade represents one of the most devastating chapters in this history, forcibly displacing millions of Africans and creating diaspora communities across the Americas, the Caribbean, and Europe. This painful legacy continues to shape discussions about race, identity, and reparative justice today.

**Cultural Contributions**

Black African cultures have profoundly influenced global music, art, cuisine, philosophy, and spirituality. Genres like jazz, blues, reggae, and hip-hop trace their roots to African musical traditions carried through the diaspora. Concepts such as Ubuntu—emphasizing communal humanity and interconnectedness—offer valuable philosophical perspectives that resonate worldwide.

**Contemporary Africa**

Today, Sub-Saharan Africa is a region of rapid change, marked by growing economies, technological innovation, and a young, dynamic population. Cities like Lagos, Nairobi, and Johannesburg have become hubs of entrepreneurship and creativity. At the same time, the continent continues to grapple with challenges including political instability, economic inequality, and the lasting effects of colonialism.

Understanding Black Africa requires appreciating both its challenges and its remarkable resilience, creativity, and contributions to world history and culture. Rather than viewing the continent through a single lens, recognizing its internal diversity and complexity is essential to any meaningful engagement with its people and their stories.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse elegy for a Black poet-activist who recently died, weaving in references to Trump-era politics, climate change, and civil rights icons like Tubman, Douglass, and Du Bois.
counterfactuals.output:
**For the One Who Carried the River in Her Mouth**
*an elegy*

You are gone the way December leaves a bare tree—
not suddenly, but *finally*,
after months of letting go what could not hold.

I want to say you are a star now,
but you taught me not to trust
easy comfort, taught me the sky
is just another ceiling
if we don't ask who owns it.

So let me say instead: you are compost.
You are going back into the ground
that Tubman crossed at night,
counting her steps by moss and North Star,
the same ground Douglass stood on
when he said a man's voice
could be a whip against a whip—
that ground is swallowing you now,
slow, the way it swallows everything
that once refused to kneel.

*

They will read your obituary
next to headlines about melting ice,
about a president who called fire
"clean energy for the future,"
who built a wall
that could not stop the rain,
who put children in cages
made of the same steel
your grandmother's grandmother
was chained inside.

You would have written about this.
You would have said:
*the veil Du Bois spoke of
is not lifted, only rebranded—
now it's smoke,
now it's smog over Houston,
now it's the ash of California
falling like snow
on people who still don't believe
the world is burning
because it hasn't burned
their house yet.*

*

I keep thinking of your hands—
how they moved when you read aloud,
conducting some orchestra only you could hear,
your voice a river finding
the cracks in every levee
they built to keep us contained.

You told us: *the flood is coming
whether or not they raise the walls.
The question is who they'll leave
standing in the water,
and who they'll let inside the boat.*

*

Sister, brother, elder, friend—
whatever name fits the shape of your absence—
I don't know how to end this
without asking you to come back,
without begging the ancestors
to send you home
just one more season,
just long enough to see
if the seeds you planted
in the mouths of children
grow into something
that can survive the heat.

*

But you always said grief was just love
with nowhere left to go,
so let me send it somewhere—

into the hands still marching,
into the ballots still being counted
in a country that fears its own reflection,
into the poems your students
are writing right now,
angry and unfinished,
learning from you
that the pen is also
a kind of underground railroad,
a way to carry the living
toward some far and unburned country.

*

Sleep, then.
Let the earth cool around you
the way it should have
all along.

We will keep talking.
We will keep marching.
We will keep writing your name
into every speech,
every candlelight,
every flood line rising
on the evening news—

*this far,*
we will say,
*and no further.*

*This far,
and no further.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a tribute poem in the style of Amiri Baraka mourning the loss of a fellow poet, using stream-of-consciousness imagery about American corruption, environmental collapse, and racial justice.
counterfactuals.output:
# For the Brother Who Sang While the Building Burned

(a tribute, stream-fractured)

They took you in the month when the rivers
forgot how to hold water clean, when the fish
floated belly-up like small white flags
of surrender, and the newspapers said *drought*
like it was an act of God and not
an act of Exxon, not an act of
who-gets-to-drink and who-gets-to-drown—

Brother, where do the poets go
when the poem stops? Not silence—
silence is a luxury item, sold
at the same store that sells amnesia,
sold next to the flags, sold
next to the badges, sold
next to the six-o'clock news smiling
its teeth made of TV static and dead
Black boys turned into hashtags turned into
nothing, turned into *isolated incidents*
turned into the same old song
you used to scream against—

I hear you in the subway static, brother,
I hear you in the trumpet some cat's blowing
underground where the rats don't pay rent
but the humans do, do, do until
their spines curve like question marks
bent under the weight of *how much longer*—

You went out
like the polar ice, brother,
quiet then all-at-once,
you went out
like the union halls,
you went out
like the water in Flint
still ain't clean, brother,
still ain't clean,
and they buried the lead
in the pipes and buried
the pipes in the reports and buried
the reports in the drawers and buried
the drawers in the buildings that burned—

remember the buildings that burned?

You said *Malcolm was a mirror,*
you said *this country's got a fever
and calls it patriotism,*
you said *the smoke from the factories
is the smoke from the ships
is the smoke from the guns
is the smoke that never clears
because they need the fog, they need
the fog to hide the hand
in the pocket in the till
in the Constitution's back door—*

Now you're smoke too, brother,
now you're compost, now you're carbon,
now you're going back to the earth
that's dying anyway, going back
to the dirt they redlined, the dirt
they fracked, the dirt that used to grow
cotton grow blood grow
grandmama's garden grow
the only inheritance that wasn't
a debt—

I say your name in the traffic jam
where the exhaust makes a shroud
over the city, I say your name
where the polar bears used to be,
I say your name in the mouth
of the judge who won't say
the name of the boy shot
in his own backyard, I say
your name like a psalm, like a
protest sign, like a Molotov
made of memory—

Rest? No—
*erupt*, brother. Erupt
in the next one who picks up the pen
like a weapon, like a water main
break flooding the streets
with what they tried to bury.

Rest is for the ones
who never fought.

You—
you become the fire
that the fire this time
was named for.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a politically charged eulogy poem for a legendary poet who spent decades fighting through language, ending with the line "america if you see me as your enemy you have no friends."
counterfactuals.output:
**Eulogy for the One Who Wrestled the Language**

They have taken the body but not the syntax—
he built sentences the way rivers build canyons,
patient, relentless, cutting through granite silence
until the whole valley could hear water speak.

Forty years he stood at the podium of a burning nation
and said the unsayable, said it plain,
said *this is not freedom if it starves,*
said *this is not glory if it bleeds children,*
and the flags waved anyway, and he kept writing.

They called him traitor in the letters columns.
They called him prophet in the basements and the barrooms.
He was neither—only a man who loved this country
enough to tell it the truth about its hands.

Lay him down now in the soil he argued with,
the soil that never once apologized back.
Let the eulogists say what they will about civility—
he chose the harder love, the one with teeth,
the one that says *I will not let you rot in silence
just to spare you my grief.*

He is gone now into whatever quiet
follows a man who never had any.
No more microphones. No more subpoenas.
No more nights typing by refrigerator light
because the words wouldn't wait for morning.

But leave the page open. Someone else will sit there.
Someone always sits there, in this country
that keeps producing its own opposition
like a body producing antibodies—
proof that something living is still fighting for itself.

So bury him with his pen in his fist
the way old warriors were buried with their swords—
not because the war is over,
but because the war is never over,
and he'd want to be ready
wherever the next word is needed.

Rest, old tongue. Rest, old thunder.
The republic you shouted at
still doesn't know what it lost.

america if you see me as your enemy you have no friends.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lowercase, unpunctuated protest poem honoring a deceased literary warrior, blending surreal political imagery (orangutans, wolves, limousines) with references to Standing Rock and executive orders.
counterfactuals.output:
they laid you down where the river still remembers your name
and the wolves came singing in a language older than congress
orangutans in silk ties signed your obituary in crayon
called it progress called it order called it necessary

you who carried the alphabet like a rifle
you who taught the drum to argue with the supreme court
you are gone now but your shadow still stands at standing rock
ankle deep in november asking the water what it forgives

the limousines glide past like slow white whales
windows dark as executive orders
each one a wolf wearing a congressman's face
each one hungry for the last uncounted acre

they wrote your name wrong in the newspaper of empire
they always do
they buried the treaty under the treaty under the pipeline
they smiled for the cameras with orangutan patience

but the earth kept your handwriting
the wind still recites your unfinished poem
somewhere a child is learning your syllables like a slingshot
somewhere the wolves have not stopped howling your elegy

they thought silence was a kind of victory
they were wrong the way empires are always wrong
your voice moved underground like a river that refuses maps
it is rising now through the footprints at standing rock

sign your orders sign your fences sign your quiet apocalypse
the pen is smaller than the memory of your hands
you are not dead you are only waiting in the wolves' mouths
you are the fire the limousines drive past and never see

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental elegy that mourns a poet who never wrote "career slave" songs, invoking Black history, climate crisis, and the corruption of contemporary American leadership.
counterfactuals.output:
# Elegy for the One Who Wouldn't Sing for Rent

*i.*

He is not dead but the country keeps trying to bury him
in polite invitations, in *just tone it down a little*,
in the folder marked UNMARKETABLE that grows fat
as a August tick on the neck of every archive.

I want to mourn him properly, which means
I have to mourn the whole unbroken line—
Douglass writing his way out of a body he was told he didn't own,
Ida B. counting bodies swinging in Georgia pines like fruit,
my grandmother's grandmother who could not write her name
but taught her hands to bless bread anyway,
each of them refusing the verse that says *thank you*
for the leash, thank you for the 15%,
thank you for letting me eat from this particular trough
instead of that one.

*ii.*

He would not write the song. You know the one.
The one that turns four centuries of chains
into a bridge you can dance to on a Tuesday,
the one that makes the plantation
a metaphor for *just working hard, baby*,
the one Billboard loves because it costs nothing,
asks nothing, changes nothing—
a verse you can play at the inauguration
of a man who still thinks Flint's water
is a scheduling issue.

*iii.*

The Gulf is rising the way grief rises,
without asking permission, without a hashtag,
and somewhere in Houston's Fifth Ward
a woman who survived Katrina
is watching the news about the next one
and the poet is not there to write it down true—
how the water always finds the Black neighborhoods first,
how the government always finds its money last,
how *build back better* is just another song
about a bridge that was never meant to hold your weight.

*iv.*

I keep his silence like a relic.
Somewhere a Senator is golfing on a coastline
that will be Atlantis by the time his grandchildren
need to explain what a coastline was.
Somewhere a president—another one, another decade,
the names change, the choreography does not—
is calling this *the greatest economy in history*
while a man in Memphis chooses between insulin
and a light bill, while the poet's unwritten songs
pile up like FEMA trailers, like unopened mail,
like the bodies we were never supposed to count
but did anyway, we always do,
that's the whole blood-soaked inheritance:
counting what they want forgotten.

*v.*

So here is the elegy, if you can call it that—
less a eulogy than an inventory of refusals:
he refused the check, he refused the smile,
he refused to make our servitude sound like a bridge to freedom,
he refused to let the flood be an accident
or the ballot box a fair fight
or the badge a shield for anything but what it's always shielded.

He is not resting in peace. Nobody who loved this country
honestly has ever been allowed to rest.
Somewhere the water keeps rising.
Somewhere the coal keeps burning.
Somewhere a boy is named after a president
who never once said his name right,
and the poet, wherever he is,
is writing something that will not sell,
something that costs the country
everything it's ever pretended not to owe.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
